== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:90
- P-76 **An integer numeral has a type of its own, `IntLiteral`, which each number type converts from: in the interpreter's library now, and under walk once walk has the checker's static types.** The design is the compiler's prelude's working one, taken in place of the specification's numeral types, which the team left unfinished. Why the split: walk has no static types, so it would give a list of numerals the element type `IntLiteral`, with no declared type to go by. The interpreter's library declares `IntLiteral`, the conversions from it into the five integer types, `QQ` and `RR64`, and `IntLiteral`'s own arithmetic, which the team had left commented out until coercion existed. Walk still gives an integer numeral the type `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, so no numeral reaches `IntLiteral`'s declarations under walk. Walk gaps: a numeral that walk matches as a `ZZ32` in a `typecase` or an overload (row 79), a numeral at an `NN32` or `NN64` binding (row 454), an integer numeral beyond `ZZ32`'s range at an `RR64` binding (row 443), a `nat` parameter used as a value (row 486), and coercion through tuple and varargs parameters (rows 395 and 511).

POSITIONS.md:92
- P-78 **`SUM` and `PROD` are one generic reduction each over the library's algebra, in place of the team's catch-all over `Number`, and take their identity from the static argument.** `SUM` is generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `PROD` over `MultiplicativeRing`. A reduction written with generators writes its static argument where nothing at the call fixes the element type. The compiled checker fixes it from neither the generators, the body nor a declared type that receives the value, and refuses every such `SUM` or `PROD` that leaves it out (row 731, a gap of the checker). Row 731's workaround is to write it in every clause form of `SUM` and `PROD`, as in `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. A sum without generators is written as before, with no static argument: `SUM e` over a collection `e`, and the dot product `x DOT y`. `BIG MAXN`, `BIG MINN` and `BIG MINMAXN`, the team's `Number`-typed big operators for the maximum, the minimum and both, each with an identity, are gone; no program called them. `MAX` and `MIN` get no identity on the integers or the floats, so an empty `BIG MAX` or `BIG MIN` raises `EmptyReduction` (F-60: a maximum's identity is its type's least value, which a coercion into a wider type does not carry). Under walk, an empty `SUM` or `PROD` over another algebra, such as a user `AdditiveGroup`, still fails (row 436) until the specification's `HasIdentity` is built.

POSITIONS.md:88
- P-74 **Mixed integer widths convert by declared coercions: each wider integer type declares a `coerce` from each narrower integer type, as the compiler prelude does.** A conversion that is exact is implicit, and a conversion that can lose precision is written out. So `ZZ32` values and integer numerals coerce into `RR64` implicitly, and a `ZZ64` value into `RR64` is written out (P-66, Java's defaults corrected where they lose precision). A call of a generic function with arguments of mixed widths infers, on both paths, the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce. A range is over `ZZ32` only (P-77, the rule on ranges). The specification's `widens` declaration, which would make a narrow computation stored into a wide variable run wide, is deferred. The implicit coercion of `NN32` into `RR64`: P-75 holds it, with its conflict with the overloads of `RR64` and `ZZ64`.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:75
- P-169 **The runtime's own 45 native bindings, the arrays' store, threads with `abort`, the task trace and the numerals, name compiled helpers that walk's loader answers with walk's own operations, P-167's device, in three compiled shapes.** Each keeps P-58's form, a bare `builtinPrimitive("…")` naming a helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the compiled path runs; walk's loader answers the name with walk's glue, so walk keeps its `AtomicArray` store, its `spawn` and its numerals, and for these names P-58's walk half bends, as for P-167's two. The arrays' 7, of `PrimitiveArray`, `PrimImmutableArray` and `PrimImmutableRR64Array`: the compiled half by P-164's device, a store trait in `FortressLibrary` whose bindings name helpers of a new `nativeHelpers/arrayOps` over a compiled class that holds the elements; `PrimitiveArray` and `PrimImmutableArray` leave the native component and hold the store in a field, and walk's native object below the trait holds an `AtomicArray`; `PrimImmutableRR64Array`'s two move onto a compiled `double[]` class that no factory chooses until array decision A (P-84, P-85). The compiled store is an `Object[]`, and the compiled transaction tracks its reads and writes by the array and the index (`TXReadSlot`, `TXWriteSlot`): P-84 stores every number type's array unboxed, so a compiled `atomic` write into any array needs that keying, and an array of objects keeps one box an element, not two. Threads, `abort` and the task trace, 6: helpers in a `nativeHelpers` class over the compiled runtime, as the team's `nativeHelpers/runtime.java` is; `Thread`'s `val`, `wait`, `ready` and `stop` raise until the code generator compiles `spawn` (row 82). The numerals, 32: `IntLiteral`'s 8 conversions and comparisons become Fortress text over its `asZZ` before the names batch; the other 24, `IntLiteral`'s 21 and `FloatLiteral`'s 3, name helpers that compute, not the prelude's raising stubs (row 318), at the names batch after a reading review designs their carrier, and walk's loader answers them by one rule per helper class, not by a table of names, still refusing a misspelt name. A test on both paths holds the two halves together where both run; `IntLiteral`'s 29 keep only walk's load check, since no walk numeral is an `IntLiteral` (P-76). Why: every array, vector, varargs list and `args` of the one library is built on `PrimitiveArray` or `PrimImmutableArray`, and a body left on glue compiles to the library's own `builtinPrimitive`, which fails, so by the code's reading a compiled program would raise at its first array; walk's loader carries no element, `Thread` or literal (F-299), and an `Object` carrier would take walk's array writes out of walk's transactions. Detail: `reviews/natives-device-2026-11-07.md`, sections 3.1 to 3.4; the store's shape: `coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-28.md`, "The questions for the curator, before the launch", Q2.

POSITIONS.md:45
- P-48 **A type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix takes its bound, never `Bottom`.** The arguments leave a parameter unfixed when it occurs only in the result type; when two arguments meet at it with no narrowest type into which both convert (a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` have one, `ZZ64`, by P-74); or when dispatch, at run time, picks a generic declaration and must choose the instance to run. Its instance is then the intersection of its upper bounds (`Any` if it has none). At checking, that is narrowed by what the call's expected type (P-49 defines it) requires of the declared return type; at run time, by the static type that the checker gave the call. It is never `Bottom`, never the union of the arguments' types, and never the value's type alone. The rule sets the instance, not which declaration runs (P-46). Why: the rule is the team's later word, from the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch, and the curator trusts the team's later work above his own understanding. The rule changes nothing in microGPT, whose types are concrete. The library keeps the team's declarations of `fail`, `builtinPrimitive` and `List`'s empty comprehension, whose type parameters have no written bound, without the `extends Object` that a batch had added. Under walk, which has no static types, dispatch takes the value's type. Row 538: a compiled dispatcher that carries the static type that the checker gave the call, so that a generic declaration reached only at run time gets this instance. Rows 587, 591 and 612: three cases in which walk still gives `Bottom`.

== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## The checker and the one library

FACTS.md:76
- F-79 **In the interpreter's library, `IntLiteral`, the type that the compiled checker gives an integer numeral, is declared on the model of the compiler's prelude: a sibling of the number types under `Number`, which each integer type, `QQ`, `RR64` and `AnyIntegral` convert from by coercion.** It builds the library half of P-76. Under walk a numeral is still a `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ`, so no numeral reaches these declarations until walk's half is built (F-74). `IntLiteral` declares itself the members of `Integral[\I\]` that a numeral could not reach, among them the getters `zero` and `one`, `odd`, `even`, `floor` and `DIVIDES`. There are three reasons: for some, no declaration of `Integral` applies to a sibling type even with coercion; for others, the declarations that apply by coercion tie; and a getter must be the type's own member. Each integer type declares its own comparisons, `CMP`, `MAXNUM` and `MINNUM`, and a `^` with an `IntLiteral` exponent. Without them, a typed integer with a numeral operand ties between a declaration inherited from a generic trait and the same operator's own declarations in `ZZ64`, `QQ` and `RR64`. The compiled checker refuses `(3).minimum` and `(3).maximum`, `ZZ32`'s getters (row 581). Gated under walk by `tests/IntegerOrderNumerals.fss`, which checks each integer type's own comparisons, `MAXNUM` and `MINNUM`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-numeral-library/REPORT.md` sections 4 and 6.

content.content:
\chaplabel{type-inference}

A call of a function, a method or an operator whose declaration has static
parameters, or of the constructor of an object that has static parameters,
need not write its static arguments, and most calls do not
(\secref{idn-ref}, \secref{dotted-method-calls}).
The static arguments of a call that does not write them are inferred
statically.
This chapter describes that inference for type parameters (\secref{type-param})
and for \KWD{nat} and \KWD{int} parameters (\secref{natparams}); the inference
of the static arguments of other kinds of static parameter, and the inference
over a whole program of the types that declarations elide
(\secref{type-inference-components}), are not yet described.
\revision{revival-inference}{The Working Draft of February 2011 left this
chapter a heading and two draft notes, the second of which is kept at its end,
although \chapref{multiple-dispatch}, \secref{idn-ref} and
\secref{dotted-method-calls} cite it.
The rule this chapter states is the one the revival decided on 26, 27 and
28~September 2026, and on 29~September 2026 for a lone type parameter with no
narrowest candidate; the compiled type checker was built with this text, and
the cases in which it departs from the text are listed in
\secref{revival-inference}.
The Working Draft had no counterpart to the rule for a numeral whose
conversions tie (\secref{numeral-default}).
A type parameter declared without an \KWD{extends} clause is bounded by
\TYP{Any} (\secref{type-param}), on the compiled path as in the interpreter.
\chapref{multiple-dispatch} and \chapref{overloaded-declarations} were revised
with this chapter's order, a declaration chosen on the parameter types it
declares and then instantiated (\secref{revival-overloading}).
The team's later Types chapter gives the coercion relation and the valid
instantiations of a quantified type, and says nothing of inference.}

\section{The Static Arguments of a Call}
\seclabel{static-arg-inference}

The static arguments of a call that does not write them are found in two
steps: the declaration that the call invokes is chosen first, and it is
instantiated second.

\emph{Choice.}
The declaration is chosen as \secref{resolving-coercion} describes.
A declaration with static parameters is applicable to a call, without or with
coercion, if some instance of it whose static arguments satisfy their bounds is
applicable to the call.
Declarations are compared on the parameter types they declare, a declaration
with static parameters on its parameter types taken over every instance that
its bounds allow, and not on an instance inferred for the call.
So a coercion is applied only to make a call possible: it never changes which
declaration is chosen when one is applicable to the call without it.

\emph{Instantiation.}
The static arguments of the chosen declaration are then inferred, and with them
the instance of the declaration that the call invokes:
\begin{itemize}
\item A type parameter, or a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter, that the
declared type of a parameter mentions other than as the whole type, as
\EXP{b\COLON\TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} mentions \VAR{T}, is fixed by
the argument at that position, whose type must be a subtype of the parameter
type of the instance.
\item Where the call has an expected type (below), a type parameter that the
declared return type mentions other than as the whole type is fixed by the
expected type as well.
\item A type parameter that is the whole declared type of one or more
parameters, as \VAR{T} is of \EXP{x\COLON{}T}, and that is not fixed as above,
takes, among the types of the arguments at those positions and the types to
which they can be coerced, the narrowest under $\morespecificeq$
(\secref{resolving-coercion}) that every one of those arguments is
substitutable for (\secref{applicability-with-coercion}) and that the bounds of
the type parameter permit.
For number arguments this is the narrowest type into which every one of them
converts: \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} for a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, and also for a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and an
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, though neither of them is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}
(\secref{basic-integers}).
Where there is no such narrowest type, and the rule for numerals
(\secref{numeral-default}) does not settle the tie, the type parameter takes
the intersection of its upper bounds: its declared bound, \TYP{Any} if it has
none (\secref{type-param}), and what the expected type (below), where the call
has one, requires of the declared return type, provided the types of those
arguments are subtypes of it; none of those arguments is converted.
\revision{revival-inference}{The revival's text of 28~September 2026 gave such
a type parameter the union of the types of those arguments; on 29~September 2026
the revival took the rule by which the dispatcher of the type group's paper of
2019 instantiates a type parameter, which gives the bound.}
\item A type parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes as
above, such as a type parameter that only the return type mentions, as its whole
type, likewise takes the intersection of its upper bounds: its declared bound,
\TYP{Any} if it has none (\secref{type-param}), and what the expected type
(below), where the call has one, requires of the declared return type.
Inference never instantiates a static parameter at \TYP{BottomType}, which
programmers must not write (\secref{bottom-type}).
So, for the declaration
\EXP{\VAR{stop}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(s\COLON\TYP{String})\COLON{}T}, the
variable declaration
\EXP{x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32 = \VAR{stop}(\hbox{\rm``\STR{no}''})} instantiates
\VAR{stop} at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and the same call with no expected type
instantiates it at \TYP{Any}.
\revision{revival-inference}{The revival's text of 28~September 2026 did not
describe such a type parameter and left open whether inference may give it
\TYP{BottomType}, which the team's draft note at the end of this chapter asks.
The revival decided on 29~September 2026 that the rule by which the dispatcher of
the type group's paper of 2019 instantiates a type parameter that the arguments
do not fix, the intersection of its upper bounds, which never instantiates a
type parameter at \TYP{BottomType}, is the rule of static inference as well.}
\item Every argument is then admitted against the corresponding parameter type
of the instance by substitutability: an argument whose type is a subtype of it
is passed as it is, and any other argument is coerced to it
(\secref{coercion}), as an argument is coerced to the declared type of a
parameter of a declaration without static parameters.
\end{itemize}
The coercions that the instance needs are inserted into the call statically,
as is any coercion that \secref{resolving-coercion} chooses.

\emph{The expected type.}
A call has an expected type in these contexts: as the right-hand side of a
variable or field declaration that declares its type, that type; as the
right-hand side of an assignment to a variable whose type is declared, that
type; as the body of a functional that declares its return type, that type;
as the last expression of a block that has an expected type, whether or not
local declarations precede it in the block, the block's expected type; as a
branch of an \KWD{if} expression with an \KWD{else} clause that has an
expected type, the expected type of the \KWD{if} expression; as a clause of an
\KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else} clause, \TYP{()}, the type that

\KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else} clause, \TYP{()}, the type that
every such clause must have (\secref{if-expr}); as a clause of a
\KWD{typecase} expression that has an expected type, its \KWD{else} clause
among them, the expected type of the \KWD{typecase} expression, of which the
union of the types of its clauses, the type of the \KWD{typecase} expression
(\secref{typecase}), is then a subtype where the type of each clause is;
as the body of a \KWD{label} expression that has an expected type, or as the
\KWD{with} clause expression of an \KWD{exit} expression whose target is that
\KWD{label} expression, the expected type of the \KWD{label} expression, of
which the union of the type of its body and the types of those \KWD{with}
clause values, the type of the \KWD{label} expression (\secref{label-expr}),
is then a subtype where each of those types is; and as an argument of a call
that this section does not accept with its arguments typed without an expected
type, where the argument is itself a call with inferred static arguments, the
parameter type at the argument's position of each declaration
of the enclosing call in turn, instantiated, where that declaration has static
parameters, by the arguments that are not so typed and by the expected type of
the enclosing call alone, as described below.
The expected type is used whether the call is written by tight juxtaposition,
as \EXP{f(x)} (\secref{juxtameaning}), or by loose juxtaposition, as
\EXP{f\;x}, or as a method invocation or an operator application.
\revision{revival-expected-contexts}{The revival's text of 29~September 2026
gave the last expression of a block an expected type only where no local
declaration precedes it, and gave none to a clause of an \KWD{if} expression
without an \KWD{else} clause, to a clause of a \KWD{typecase} expression or to
a call written by loose juxtaposition; the revival decided on 8~October 2026
that each has the type that the text already requires of it.
Its text of 8~October 2026 gave none to the body of a \KWD{label} expression
or to the \KWD{with} clause expression of an \KWD{exit} expression; the
revival decided on 9~October 2026 that they have the expected type of the
\KWD{label} expression, as a clause of a \KWD{typecase} expression has that of
the \KWD{typecase} expression.
Its text of 9~October 2026 gave none to an argument of another call; the
revival decided on 9~October 2026 that an argument that is itself a call with
inferred static arguments has the parameter type of each declaration
of the enclosing call in turn where the enclosing call is not accepted without
it, since the static arguments of a call ``are statically inferred from the
context of the function call'' (\secref{idn-ref}).}
The return type of the instance that the steps above find must be a subtype of
the expected type.
If they find no such instance, the static arguments are inferred again without
the expected type, and the call is accepted only if the return type of the instance
then found is a subtype of the expected type or can be coerced to it; in the
second case the result of the call is coerced to the expected type
(\secref{coercion}).
So, for the declarations
\EXP{\VAR{wrap}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON\TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}
and \EXP{\VAR{id}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T},
the variable declaration \EXP{a\COLON\TYP{List}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}64\rrbracket = \VAR{wrap}(3)}
instantiates \VAR{wrap} at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, which the expected type fixes,
and coerces the numeral, while \EXP{b\COLON\mathbb{Z}64 = \VAR{id}(3)}
instantiates \VAR{id} at the numeral's own type (\secref{literals}) and coerces
the result.

The arguments of a call are typed first without an expected type.
Where this section then accepts no instance of the call, each argument that is
itself a call with inferred static arguments is typed again, once
for each declaration of the enclosing call, with the parameter type at its
position as its expected type, as the list of contexts above says.
Of the declarations that are applicable to the enclosing call with its
arguments so typed, each declaration with its own, and whose instances have
return types that are subtypes of the expected type of the enclosing call,
where it has one, or can be coerced to it, the enclosing call invokes the one
that is more specific than every other on the parameter types they declare;
where there is no such declaration, the call is typed with its arguments typed
without an expected type, and is accepted or refused as above.
So where this section accepts an instance of a call with its arguments typed
without an expected type, no argument is typed again, and the declaration it
invokes is never passed over for one that only an argument typed again makes
applicable; a declaration that is applicable to those arguments but whose
return type neither is a subtype of the expected type nor can be coerced to it
is not accepted, and another may then be chosen.
For example, for the declarations
\EXP{\VAR{mk}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket()\COLON\TYP{Box}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket},
\EXP{\VAR{takes}(b\COLON\TYP{Box}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}64\rrbracket)},
\EXP{\VAR{over}(b\COLON\TYP{Box}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}64\rrbracket)} and
\EXP{\VAR{over}(x\COLON\TYP{Any})}, the call \EXP{\VAR{takes}(\VAR{mk}())}
instantiates \VAR{mk} at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, which the parameter type of
\VAR{takes} fixes, while the call \EXP{\VAR{over}(\VAR{mk}())} invokes the
second declaration of \VAR{over}, which is applicable to \EXP{\VAR{mk}()} typed
without an expected type, the instance of \VAR{mk} at the bound of its type
parameter.
\revision{revival-expected-contexts}{The revival's text of 9~October 2026 had
no such paragraph; the revival added it with the argument of a call to the list
of contexts above, following its decision of 9~October 2026.}

\emph{Dispatch.}
The call, with the coercions of its instance inserted, dispatches at run time
as \secref{resolving-overloading} describes, by subtyping and without further
coercion, to the most specific declaration applicable to the converted values.

For example, of the declarations
\EXP{\VAR{op}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Number}\rrbracket(a\COLON{}T, b\COLON{}T)}
and \EXP{\VAR{op}(a\COLON\TYP{Any}, b\COLON\TYP{Any})}, the call
\EXP{\VAR{op}(z, w)}, where \VAR{z} has type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \VAR{w} has
type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, chooses the first, which is applicable without
coercion, since its instance at \TYP{Number} is, and is more specific than the
second; the first is instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \VAR{z} is coerced,
and the converted call runs that instance.
\revision{revival-inference}{The interpreter has no static types and applies
the same rule at dispatch, from the run-time types of the arguments: it infers
the static arguments of a declaration with static parameters with coercion,
and instantiates the declaration that its dispatch chooses by the rule for a
type parameter that is a parameter's whole type.
So where the declared type of a variable is wider than the type of its value,
or an argument's static type is \TYP{Any}, it may run a declaration at a
narrower instance than the compiled path, which instantiates it at the static
types.
Where neither an argument's type nor a type into which the arguments convert is
the narrowest, it gives a type parameter that is the whole type of parameters
its declared bound, \TYP{Any} if it has none, as this chapter does: for a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, \TYP{Number} where that is the
bound and \TYP{Any} where the type parameter is declared without an
\KWD{extends} clause.
It does the same where the arguments that fix a type parameter inside other
types, as the results of two function arguments do, have several minimal common
supertypes.
Neither holds of a type parameter whose bound mentions a static parameter,
itself or another, or that is declared with several bounds that the interpreter
cannot meet, as it cannot meet two bounds neither of which is a subtype of the
other: such a type parameter it binds, as before, to the narrowest named common
supertype of the arguments' run-time types that the bounds permit, where there
is one, and where there is none a call that fixes a type parameter of the
second kind fails (row~591 of the revival's gap ledger).
When its dispatch chooses among declarations, it passes over a declaration with
static parameters whose arguments have several minimal common supertypes in
favour of any other declaration applicable to the call without coercion
(row~589 of the revival's gap ledger).
It fixes a type parameter by the expected type only at a reduction or a
comprehension that writes no static argument and whose value is that of a
local variable declared with a type or of a top-level or local function
declared with a return type, as the box after the list in
\secref{numeral-default} says; elsewhere it does not yet fix a type parameter
by the expected type.
A type parameter that an argument bounds only from above, as a function
argument bounds the type parameter of its parameter type, it instantiates at the
intersection of the upper bounds that its declared bound and the arguments
place on it: at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} for a function of a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} where
the type parameter is declared without an \KWD{extends} clause, and at
\TYP{Number} for a function of an \TYP{Any} where it is bounded by
\TYP{Number}; such a type parameter whose bound mentions a
static parameter, or that is declared with several bounds that it cannot meet,
it still instantiates at \TYP{BottomType}; and where the arguments place on
such a type parameter two upper bounds that it cannot meet, as a function over
one trait and a function over another do when neither trait extends the other,
the call fails with an error of unification (row~616 of the revival's gap ledger).
It infers the static arguments of a generic dotted method that a call does not
write as it infers a generic function's, whether the method is alone under its
name or among the overloads of its receiver.
It compares declarations with static parameters on the parameter types they
declare, but for two kinds: a functional method of a generic trait or object it
compares on the instance that a call makes, and a generic dotted method on the
parameter types it declares only where exactly one of the two declarations'
declared parameter types lies inside the other's, and otherwise on that instance.
It stops at load on an object or trait that declares a generic dotted method
beside a plain one of the same name (row~760 of the revival's gap ledger), and
it stops on an object that extends a generic trait whose dotted method has a
static parameter of its own bounded by the trait's, at load or at a generic
object's first instance (row~762).
It reads the bounds of a generic method that a trait declares, and the types
into which the arguments convert, where the trait declares the method, as it
reads those of a method that an object declares.
It dispatches a converted call again, except a call of an overloaded method.}

Every expression has a \emph{static type},
and every value has a \emph{runtime type}
(also known as a \emph{dynamic type}).
Fortress programs are checked before they are executed to ensure that if
an expression $e$ evaluates to a value $v$, the runtime type of $v$ is a
subtype of the static type of $e$.
Sometimes we abuse terminology by saying that
an expression has the runtime type of the value it evaluates to
(see \secref{eval-completion} for a discussion about evaluation of expressions).

Some types may be parameterized by \emph{static parameters};
we call these types \emph{generic types}.
See \chapref{trait-parameters} for a discussion of static parameters.
A static parameter may be instantiated with a type or a value
depending on whether it is a type parameter.
\note{
Victor: I don't know if the follow really belongs here.
It isn't complete in any case, because of union/intersection types.}
Two types are identical if and only if they are the same kind and
their names and static arguments (if any) are identical.
Two \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} static arguments
(\secref{natparams}, \secref{static-expr})
are identical if and only if they are written alike
once each operation whose operands are numerals is replaced by its value:
\EXP{2\;3} and \EXP{6} are identical,
and \EXP{s_{0}\;s_{1}} is identical to itself but not to \EXP{s_{1}\;s_{0}}.
Two such arguments are known to differ when they are two different numerals;
a static parameter, or an expression in which one occurs,
\TYP{BottomType} is the bottom of the type hierarchy:
all types are supertypes of \TYP{BottomType}.
For types $T$ and $U$,
we write $T \Ovrsubtype U$ when $T$ is a subtype of $U$,
and $T \strictsubtype U$ when $T \Ovrsubtype U$ and $T \neq U$;
in the latter case,
we say $T$ is a \emph{strict} subtype of $U$.
We also say that $T$ is a \emph{supertype} of $U$ if $U$ is a subtype of $T$.
Thus, in the execution of a
valid Fortress program, an expression's runtime type is always a subtype of
its static type.
We say that a value is \emph{an instance of} its runtime
type and of every supertype of its runtime type; immediate subtypes of
\TYP{Any} comprises of tuple types, arrow types, \TYP{()}, \TYP{Object}, and
\TYP{Index}, the trait of the types that a subscript takes, of which a tuple
type whose element types are all subtypes of \TYP{Index} is a subtype
(\secref{tuple-types}).
\revision{revival-index}{The Working Draft of February 2011 listed tuple
types, arrow types, \TYP{()} and \TYP{Object} only; \TYP{Index}, which
extends \TYP{Any} and not \TYP{Object}, is new.}

\begin{Fortress}
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
\end{Fortress}
where $v$ is the value of the $n$-digit numeral, with the radix point
deleted, interpreted in radix $r$.

Every numeral also has type
\EXP{\TYP{Numeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n}, \VAR{m}, \VAR{r}, and \VAR{v}.


Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types
because, as in common mathematical usage,
we expect them to be polymorphic.
For example, consider the numeral \EXP{3.1415926535897932384};
converting it immediately to a floating-point number
may lose precision.
If that numeral is used in an expression
involving floating-point intervals,
it would be better to convert it directly to an interval.
Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
in Fortress).
\Library\ define coercions
from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
and rational numbers (for compound numerals).
In \library, every numeral without a radix point has the type
\TYP{IntLiteral}, which extends \TYP{Number} and none of the number types
(\secref{basic-rationals}); each of the five integer types
(\secref{basic-integers}), \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} declares a
coercion from it.
\revision{revival-numeral-type}{The Working Draft of February 2011 described
the numeral types above, which no library declares, and did not name the type
that \library\ give a numeral.
The revival decided on 29~September 2026 that a numeral has a type of its own,
\TYP{IntLiteral}, from which each number type converts, the type the compiled
path's own library gives it, and \library\ now declare it so.
The compiled type checker gives every numeral without a radix point that type.
The interpreter does not yet: it gives such a numeral the type
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its value
does not fit in the narrower type, and it is to give it the type
\TYP{IntLiteral} once it runs with the static types of the compiled type
checker.}


\marginnote{What is an ``integer'' in this context?}
In Fortress, dividing two integers using the $/$ operator produces
a \emph{rational number};\marginnote{Not if the second integer is 0.}
this is true regardless of whether
the integers are of type $\mathbb{Z}$ (or \txt{ZZ}),
$\mathbb{Z}64$ (or \txt{ZZ64}), $\mathbb{N}32$ (or \txt{NN32}), or
whatever.  Addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of rationals
are always exact; thus values such as \EXP{1/3} are represented exactly in
Fortress.

\note{We should give an example with a radix specifier.}
Numerals containing a radix point are actually rational
literals; thus \EXP{3.125} has the rational value \EXP{3125/1000}.
The quotient of two integer literals is a static expression
(described in \secref{static-expr}) whose value is rational.
Similarly, a sequence of digits with a radix point followed by the symbol
$\times$ and an integer literal raised to an integer literal,
such as \EXP{6.0221415 \times 10^{23}}
is a static expression whose value is rational.
If such static expressions are mentioned as part of a floating-point
computation, the compiler performs the rational arithmetic exactly and then
converts the result to a floating-point value, thus incurring
at most one floating-point rounding error.
But in general rational computations may also be performed at run time,
not just at compile time.
\note{This specifies too much about the implementation:
I don't think we should mention a compiler at all, except perhaps as informal discussion.
In particular, wouldn't it be correct if this arithmetic were actually deferred and
performed exactly at run time?}


A rational number can be thought of as a pair of integers $p$ and $q$
that have been reduced to ``standard form in lowest terms'';
that is, $q > 0$ and there is no nonzero integer $k$
such that $p \over k$ and $q \over k$ are integers
and $\left| {p \over k} \right| + \left| {q \over k} \right|
	< \left| p \right| + \left| q \right|$.
The type $\mathbb{Q}$ includes all such rational numbers.
Relaxing the requirement $q>0$ to $q \geq 0$ adds three more values, which
$\mathbb{Q}$ also includes: \EXP{1/0} and \EXP{-1/0}, the infinite rationals,
and \EXP{0/0}, the indefinite rational.
\marginnote{Is there any subtyping or coercion relationship between \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}*}?
If \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}*}
then static checking would normally disallow the assignment,
so is this a relaxation to that rule?  If so, the static checker needs to know about it.}
The advantage of these values is that $\mathbb{Q}$ is closed under the rational
operations $+$, $-$, $\times$, and $/$.
In ASCII, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} is written as \txt{QQ}.
See \secref{basic-rationals} for its operations.
\revision{revival-literals}{The Working Draft of February 2011 described
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}} as three types,
said that a value of type \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} assigned to a variable of type
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} throws a \TYP{DivisionByZero} at run time if it is \EXP{1/0}
or \EXP{-1/0}, gave the ASCII names \txt{QQ\_star} and \txt{QQ\_splat}, and
pointed to \secref{advanced-rationals} for the definitions.
The three are one type now, as in \library\ (\secref{basic-rationals}), so no
such assignment converts or throws; that is also the answer to the margin
note's question whether \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} are related by
subtyping or by coercion.}

\section{A Numeral Whose Conversions Tie}
\seclabel{numeral-default}

A numeral has a type of its own, from which \library\ define coercions to the
number types (\secref{literals}).
Where the types to which a numeral can be converted are incomparable under
$\morespecificeq$, as \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} are, each
taking a numeral and neither converting into the other, the numeral is read as
a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its
value does not fit in the narrower type.
This holds in either step: in the choice among declarations that are applicable
to the call only with coercion and that the numeral would otherwise leave tied,
and in the instantiation of a type parameter that only numerals fix.
So of the declarations \EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{N}32)} and
\EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32)}, the call \EXP{g(0)} invokes the second; and a
type parameter that only numerals fix, whose bounds \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} satisfy and the numeral's own type does not, is
instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} when \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} holds the numerals'
values.

The rule settles only a tie that a numeral makes.
Where an argument that is not a numeral leaves the declarations applicable to a
call only with coercion tied, no declaration is the most specific, and the call
is a static error.

This chapter does not yet describe:
\begin{itemize}
\item the static arguments of a \KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim}, \KWD{unit} or operator
parameter (\secref{boolparams}, \secref{dimunitparams}, \secref{opr-ident});
\item a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter that neither an argument nor the
expected type fixes;
\item the element type of a reduction that only its generator clauses determine
(\secref{reduction-expr}): the rule above gives a static parameter of the big
operator that nothing at the call fixes its bounds, not the type of the
elements;
\item whether an argument whose declared parameter type mentions a static
parameter inside another type may be converted where only a conversion of its
elements would satisfy the bounds of the parameter; under the rule above such
an argument fixes the parameter by subtyping and is not converted;
\item an expected type in any context other than those listed above, such as
the body of a \KWD{for} loop;
\item the static arguments of an object with static parameters that is named
without a call, which a program writes (\secref{where-clauses});
\item the inference over a whole program of the types that declarations elide
(\secref{type-inference-components}).
\end{itemize}
\revision{revival-expected-contexts}{The revival's text of 29~September 2026
named here also an expression that a local declaration precedes in a block, an
\KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else} clause, a \KWD{typecase} expression
and a call written by loose juxtaposition, its text of 8~October 2026 also
the body of a \KWD{label} expression, and its text of 9~October 2026 also an
argument of another call, to which the list of contexts in
\secref{static-arg-inference} now gives an expected type where the argument is
itself a call with inferred static arguments and the enclosing call
is not accepted without it.}
\revision{revival-inference}{The compiled type checker instantiates a type
parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes at the
intersection of its upper bounds, as \secref{static-arg-inference} says; on the
compiled path, as in the interpreter, a type parameter declared without an
\KWD{extends} clause is bounded by \TYP{Any}, so that a call that fixes such a
parameter by the expected type alone may fix it at a type that \TYP{Object}
excludes, such as \TYP{()}.
A reduction's big operator is an argument of the call that the reduction's
desugaring makes, so it has an expected type only as such an argument has one:
the compiled type checker instantiates a generic big operator whose static
argument the reduction does not write at its bound, and at the reduction's
expected type only where the reduction's type at that bound does not fit it,
and it refuses the reduction where the big operator has no instance at its
bound, as one whose bound mentions its own static parameter has none (row~425
of the revival's gap ledger).
The interpreter instantiates a type parameter of a function that nothing at a
call fixes at its bound, \TYP{Any} if it has none, and one whose bound mentions
other static parameters at that bound with their instances, with two
exceptions: a type parameter that only the bound of a type parameter that the
arguments fix mentions, as \EXP{A \KWD{extends} T} mentions \VAR{T}, it
instantiates at the arguments' type, not at its bound, since it has no expected
type to fix it (row~592 of the revival's gap ledger); and a type parameter
declared with several bounds that it cannot meet, as two bounds neither of which
is a subtype of the other, it erases to \TYP{BottomType} (row~591).
A type parameter whose bound mentions the type parameter itself, as the big
operators $\sum$ and $\prod$ declare theirs, and that nothing at a call fixes,
it leaves open: it does not instantiate it, and it admits every value where it
checks a value against that type, as an argument, a variable declared with that
type, a \KWD{typecase} clause or a type assertion.
The big operator that a reduction or a comprehension invokes without its
static arguments it instantiates as the desugaring by the type \VAR{N} of the
expression would (\secref{reduction-expr}), with run-time types in place of the
static type that it does not have: by the declared type of the local variable,
or the declared return type of the top-level or local function, whose value the
reduction or the comprehension is, also as the last expression of a block, where
that type fixes the big operator's result type; otherwise by the join of the run-time types of
the elements that its generator clauses give, which it collects before it
reduces them; and where there is no element, at the bound of each static
parameter, or open where the bound mentions the parameter itself.
So an empty sum that is the value of a function declared \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
is the \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} zero, and the library's set reductions
\EXP{\bigcup} and \EXP{\bigcap} run on sets of their elements' type; but an
empty reduction that no declared type directs takes the identity of
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} whatever the type of the expression, and an empty
comprehension that no declared type directs is built at the bound, a list
comprehension as a \EXP{\TYP{List}\llbracket\TYP{Any}\rrbracket} (row~716 of the
revival's gap ledger); a comprehension that no declared type reaches, such as
the value of a top-level variable, a field, a method or a function expression,
the right-hand side of an assignment, the body of another reduction or an
argument of a call, is
built at the run-time types of its elements, which the declared type of an
enclosing expression may not admit (rows~20, 510 and~717).
A big operator whose declared result is none of the library's
\TYP{BigReduction}, \TYP{Comprehension} and \TYP{BigOperator} it instantiates
through the one of those three that its declared result extends, with that
trait's static arguments.
It gives a function expression that declares no return type the return type
\TYP{BottomType}, so that a type parameter that only its result fixes is
instantiated there (row~587); and it instantiates a static parameter of a
generic method that only the expected type would fix, as one of a generic
function, at its bound (row~510), a method that a trait declares among them.
The third item of the team's draft note below asks whether inference may give a
static parameter \TYP{BottomType}; the rule of \secref{static-arg-inference},
taken from the type group's paper of 2019, answers that it may not.
Neither implementation infers a \KWD{bool} parameter yet: the compiled type
checker refuses by name to infer a \KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim} or \KWD{unit}
parameter, and the interpreter does not unify a \KWD{bool} one (row~307 of
the revival's gap ledger) and stops at load on an object or trait whose method
has a parameter type with a \KWD{bool} static argument (row~761).
The example of \secref{boolparams}, a coercion whose \KWD{bool} parameter only
its parameter type mentions, can be applied only if its argument fixes that
parameter.}

\note{ \begin{itemize}
 \item
 There seems to be a circular dependency between inference and juxtaposition
 disambiguation -- you have to know if the subexpressions have arrow types
 to disambiguate, but you can't do that without using inference, which
 requires knowing how the variable of unknown type is used.
\item Type Inference (Dan's email titled ``Comments on a first reading of the spec'' on 06/05/07)
\item Do we want to forbid such cases where type inference infers
\TYP{BottomType}s for static parameters?
 \end{itemize}
}

4:: One of the four JVMs of `ant testFast`.
7:: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.
12:## The two suites
14:`ant testFast` runs about 2,100 tests in four tracks at once, in about 5 to 7 minutes:
16:- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
17:- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
18:- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
21:`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs about 680 tests in four shards, in about 2 to 4 minutes.
23:`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in about a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.
29:The two suites work in the same way:
31:- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
33:- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
36:To run a suite:
38:- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
40:- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
41:- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.
45:Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.
47:- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
48:- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.
57:- No suite and no stage of the gate runs the team demos, the programs of `ProjectFortress/demos/`. Keep each of the 52 demos that `DemoTests` lists reaching its end (P-79). Check them with the demo driver below, not with `ant testDemos`, whose test of the output is weaker:
63:- Nothing runs these folders: `not_working_compiler_tests/`, `not_working_library_tests/`, `not_working_static_tests/`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`, `long_term_not_working/`, `linker_tests/`, `compiler_regressions/`. Put every new test in a gated test folder. A test of a defect that fails today is an `XXX` test there (`tests-writing.md`).
65:## When to run a whole suite
67:- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
70:  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
77:The suites do not check these:
80:- DSL grammars, except one program whose phases the misc track runs: `syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss`;
84:- a behaviour above one thread that one run of each suite at four threads does not hit.
94:Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:
97:        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]
99:- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
109:    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss
115:Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`).
117:The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.
119:    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
123:- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
131:    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test compiler_tests/Y.test
133:Run all the new files of one test folder together, in one JVM, as the suite does. A test that passes alone can fail beside others.

    shift(newOrigin:I):Array[\E,I\]

    fill(v:E):Array[\E,I\]

    copy():Array[\E,I\]
    replica[\U\]():Array[\U,I\]

    (** Freeze array (return mutable copy) **)
    freeze(): ImmutableArray[\E,I\]
end

(** Factory for arrays that returns an empty 0-indexed array of a given
    run-time-determined size. **)
array[\E\](x:ZZ32):Array[\E,ZZ32\] = __arr1(__thrower[\E\],reflect(x))
array[\E\](x:ZZ32,y:ZZ32):Array[\E,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] =
    __arr2(__thrower[\E\],reflect(x), reflect(y))
array[\E\](x:ZZ32,y:ZZ32,z:ZZ32):Array[\E,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] =
    __arr3(__thrower[\E\],reflect(x), reflect(y), reflect(z))

(* This should be local to array, but we don't support local
   parametric methods in the language spec at all at the moment. *)
__arr1[\E, nat n\](w:()->E,x:N[\n\]):Array1[\E,0,n\] =
    array1[\E,n\]()
__arr2[\E, nat n, nat m\](w:()->E,x:N[\n\],y:N[\m\]):
    Array2[\E,0,n,0,m\] = array2[\E,n,m\]()
  end

__thrower[\T\](): T = throw ForbiddenException(CallerViolation)

(* At each number type array1 gives a vector: a typecase over a witness of
   its result type finds the type, as in additiveIdentity, and the vector
   built at that type is returned through cast. *)
array1[\T, nat s0\]():Array1[\T,0,s0\] =
    typecase __thrower[\Array1[\T,0,s0\]\] of
        () -> Array1[\ZZ32,0,s0\] => cast[\Array1[\T,0,s0\]\](vector[\ZZ32,s0\]())
        () -> Array1[\ZZ64,0,s0\] => cast[\Array1[\T,0,s0\]\](vector[\ZZ64,s0\]())
        () -> Array1[\NN32,0,s0\] => cast[\Array1[\T,0,s0\]\](vector[\NN32,s0\]())
        () -> Array1[\NN64,0,s0\] => cast[\Array1[\T,0,s0\]\](vector[\NN64,s0\]())
        () -> Array1[\ZZ,0,s0\] => cast[\Array1[\T,0,s0\]\](vector[\ZZ,s0\]())
        () -> Array1[\QQ,0,s0\] => cast[\Array1[\T,0,s0\]\](vector[\QQ,s0\]())
        () -> Array1[\RR32,0,s0\] => cast[\Array1[\T,0,s0\]\](vector[\RR32,s0\]())
        () -> Array1[\RR64,0,s0\] => cast[\Array1[\T,0,s0\]\](vector[\RR64,s0\]())
        else => PrimitiveArray[\T,s0\]()
    end
array1[\T, nat s0\](v:T):Array1[\T,0,s0\] = array1[\T,s0\]().fill(v)
tabulatedArray1[\T, nat s0\](f:ZZ32->T):Array1[\T,0,s0\] = array1[\T,s0\]().tabulate(f)

end

trait DistributesOver[\E\] end

(** The identity of + and of juxtaposition for the number type named by the
    static argument alone, with no element in hand: the typecase over a
    %() -> T% witness, the witness of its result type, as %array1% takes
    one of its own.  Each type is tested before its supertypes. **)
additiveIdentity[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\](): T =
    typecase __thrower[\T\] of
        () -> ZZ32 =>
            v: ZZ32 = 0
            cast[\T\](v)
        () -> ZZ64 => cast[\T\](widen(0))
        () -> NN32 => cast[\T\](unsigned(0))
        () -> NN64 => cast[\T\](widen(unsigned(0)))
        () -> ZZ => cast[\T\](big(0))
        () -> QQ => cast[\T\](Ratio(0, 1))
        () -> RR32 => cast[\T\](narrow(0.0))
        () -> RR64 =>
            v: RR64 = 0.0
            cast[\T\](v)
        else => cast[\T\](0)
    end

multiplicativeIdentity[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\](): T =
    typecase __thrower[\T\] of
        () -> ZZ32 =>
            v: ZZ32 = 1
            cast[\T\](v)
        () -> ZZ64 => cast[\T\](widen(1))
        () -> NN32 => cast[\T\](unsigned(1))
        () -> NN64 => cast[\T\](widen(unsigned(1)))
        () -> ZZ => cast[\T\](big(1))
        () -> QQ => cast[\T\](Ratio(1, 1))
        () -> RR32 => cast[\T\](narrow(1.0))
        () -> RR64 =>
            v: RR64 = 1.0
            cast[\T\](v)
        else => cast[\T\](1)
    end

object SumProdReductionPair[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\] extends ReductionPair[\T,T\]
         RightRange[\(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] =
    do (x,y,z) = xyz; right3Range(x,y,z) end

opr #() : TrivialOpenRange = TrivialOpenRange

# Runs the old code, the base's: bin/fortress of the batch's one base build, with FORTRESS_HOME set to the
# base build and FORTRESS_CACHES to a private caches folder. If the folder does not exist yet, it is first
# made as a copy of the base build's default_repository/caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). The paths in those caches
# are the base build's own, so nothing is translated, and no worktree is made.
#
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss    the compiled path: compile ...
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P            ... then run
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss            walk
#
# Every cache a run writes goes to the private folder: every cache directory and the logs are under
# fortress.caches (repository/ProjectProperties.java:283-299), which FORTRESS_CACHES sets, and
# bin/fortress_classpath and bin/run_classpath put FORTRESS_CACHES/bytecode_cache on the class path.
# Under the base build a run reads the build, the library sources and default_repository/configuration, and
# writes nothing that stays: the parser writes its error logs beside each file it parses from source and
# deletes them (compiler/Parser.java:349-367), so a compile of a program that exports Executable creates and
# deletes two empty, gitignored logs beside Library/Executable.fsi. Two runs at once may share those two
# names; that is harmless, because the base's library parses without errors, so both logs stay empty and
# a log removed by the other run reads as empty (Parser.java:373-377). Measured in
# explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md, section 6.
#
# Keep the private folder and your programs outside the base build (the program's own logs go beside it).
# Refuses (exit 2) a base build that is not built, and a private folder inside the base build.
set -euo pipefail
USAGE='usage: old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...'
BASE=$(realpath "${1:?$USAGE}")
PRIV_ARG=${2:?$USAGE}
shift 2
[ -x "$BASE/bin/fortress" ] && [ -e "$BASE/ProjectFortress/build/com/sun/fortress/Shell.class" ] \
  && [ -e "$BASE/default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar" ] \
  || { echo "old-fortress: $BASE is not a built tree" >&2 ; exit 2 ; }
PRIV=$(realpath -m "$PRIV_ARG")
case "$PRIV/" in "$BASE"/*) echo "old-fortress: $PRIV is inside the base build $BASE" >&2 ; exit 2 ;; esac
if [ ! -d "$PRIV" ]; then
    mkdir -p "$(dirname "$PRIV")"
    PART="$PRIV.part.$$"
    cp -a "$BASE/default_repository/caches" "$PART"
    mv -T "$PART" "$PRIV" 2>/dev/null || rm -rf "$PART"     # another run made it first: use that one
fi
FORTRESS_HOME="$BASE" FORTRESS_CACHES="$PRIV" exec "$BASE/bin/fortress" "$@"

1	(* MicroGptFlat -- microGPT in native Fortress arrays, data designed after Hsu
     2	   (Run C4, the synthesis of rounds two and three: explorations/run-c4/design.md).
     3	   The model only: hyperparameters, the layout table, the four vector
     4	   functions, the step, Adam and the training loop, line for line against
     5	   explorations/apl/reference/hsu-flat/microgpt_concise.dyalog and the formulas
     6	   (the tour: explorations/run-c4/tour.md).  The array vocabulary is FlatArrays,
     7	   the loaders and the corpus FlatData.  Run from explorations/run-c4/src: the
     8	   paths are relative. *)
     9	component MicroGptFlat
    10	export MicroGptFlat
    11	export Executable
    12	import FlatArrays.{...}
    13	import FlatData.{...}
    14	import System.{...}
    15	
    16	(* --------------------------------------------------- hyperparameters ---- *)
    17	(nEmbd, blockSize, nHead, headDim, vocabSize, bosId) = (16, 16, 4, 4, 27, 26)
    18	(epsilon, lr0, beta1, beta2, epsilon_A, nSteps) = (10.0^(-5), 0.01, 0.85, 0.99, 10.0^(-8), 1000)
    19	(corpusPath, weightsDir) = ("../../apl/reference/dzaima/docs.txt", "../../apl/reference/dzaima/w")
    20	
    21	(* ^T on a matrix and on every plane of a rank-3 array, declared here and not
    22	   in the vocabulary because an API cannot declare a postfix operator (row 133) *)
    23	opr (m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\])^T[\nat r, nat c\]: Matrix[\RR64,c,r\] = transpose(m)
    24	opr (t: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\])^T[\nat a, nat b, nat c\]: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,c,0,b\] = transpose(t)
    25	
    26	(* -------------------------------------- rmsn, sm and their backward ------ *)
    27	rmsn(x: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = x / SQRT (epsilon + (x DOT x) / |x|)
    28	sm(z: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = do e = exp(z - (BIG MAX z)); e / (SUM e) end
    29	mask: Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = mat(blockSize, blockSize, fn (i: ZZ32, j: ZZ32): RR64 => if j > i then -(10.0^10) else 0.0 end)
    30	rmsn_b(dy: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], x: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = do
    31	    r = SQRT (epsilon + (x DOT x) / |x|); y = x / r
    32	    (dy - y ((y DOT dy) / |y|)) / r
    33	  end
    34	sm_b(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], dy: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = p × (dy - (p DOT dy))
    35	
    36	(* ------------------------------- tactic 2/8: one vector, nine views ------ *)
    37	matName(i: ZZ32): String =
    38	    if i = 0 then "wte" elif i = 1 then "wpe" elif i = 2 then "lm_head" elif i = 3 then "attn_wq" elif i = 4 then "attn_wk"
    39	    elif i = 5 then "attn_wv" elif i = 6 then "attn_wo" elif i = 7 then "mlp_fc1" else "mlp_fc2" end
    40	matShape(i: ZZ32): (ZZ32, ZZ32) =
    41	    if (i = 0) OR (i = 2) then (vocabSize, nEmbd) elif i = 7 then (4 nEmbd, nEmbd) elif i = 8 then (nEmbd, 4 nEmbd) else (nEmbd, nEmbd) end
    42	matCount(i: ZZ32): ZZ32 = do (r, c) = matShape(i); r c end
    43	matOffset(i: ZZ32): ZZ32 = SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#i] matCount(j)
    44	nParams(): ZZ32 = matOffset(9)
    45	view(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], i: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do (r, c) = matShape(i); view(p, matOffset(i), r, c) end
    46	
    47	(* -------------------- tactic 3/5: the corpus as one padded integer matrix - *)
    48	corpus: Corpus = loadCorpus(corpusPath, blockSize, bosId)
    49	
    50	(* ------------------------- the step: keys -> (loss, flat gradient). Pure. -- *)
    51	step(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], b: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\]): (RR64, Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]) = do
    52	    ids = corpus.tokens(b, 0); tg = corpus.tokens(b, 1); vm = corpus.valid(b); nv = SUM vm; pos = corpus.positions(b)
    53	    (wte, wpe, lm, wq, wk, wv, wo, f1, f2) = (view(p, 0), view(p, 1), view(p, 2), view(p, 3), view(p, 4), view(p, 5), view(p, 6), view(p, 7), view(p, 8))
    54	    h(m: Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = heads(m, blockSize, nHead, headDim)
    55	    u(t: Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = unheads(t, nHead)
    56	    (* -- forward, all (doc, pos) rows at once -- *)
    57	    x = gather(wte, ids) + gather(wpe, pos); xp = rows(rmsn, x); x1 = rows(rmsn, xp)
    58	    (q, k, v) = (x1 wq^T, x1 wk^T, x1 wv^T); (qh, kh, vh) = (h(q), h(k), h(v))
    59	    a = rows(sm, mask + (qh kh^T) / SQRT (1.0 headDim)); hc = u(a vh)
    60	    x2 = xp + hc wo^T; x3 = rows(rmsn, x2); m0 = x3 f1^T; mr = 0.0 MAX m0; x4 = x2 + mr f2^T
    61	    pr = rows(sm, x4 lm^T); loss = -(vm DOT log(pick(pr, tg))) / nv
    62	    (* -- backward, one line under each forward line, bottom-up -- *)
    63	    dL = diag(vm / nv) (pr - onehot(tg, vocabSize)); gLM = dL^T x4; dX4 = dL lm
    64	    gF2 = dX4^T mr; dM0 = (dX4 f2) × (m0 > 0.0); gF1 = dM0^T x3; dX3 = dM0 f1
    65	    dX2 = dX4 + rows(rmsn_b, dX3, x2); gWO = dX2^T hc; dh = h(dX2 wo)
    66	    dVh = a^T dh; dS = rows(sm_b, a, dh vh^T) / SQRT (1.0 headDim)
    67	    dQh = dS kh; dKh = dS^T qh; (dQ, dK, dV) = (u(dQh), u(dKh), u(dVh))
    68	    (gWQ, gWK, gWV) = (dQ^T x1, dK^T x1, dV^T x1); dX1 = dQ wq + dK wk + dV wv
    69	    dXp = dX2 + rows(rmsn_b, dX1, xp); dX = rows(rmsn_b, dXp, x)
    70	    gWTE = transpose(onehot(ids, vocabSize)) dX; gWPE = transpose(onehot(pos, blockSize)) dX
    71	    (loss, flat(gWTE, gWPE, gLM, gWQ, gWK, gWV, gWO, gF1, gF2))
    72	  end
    73	
    74	(* --------------------- Adam: three whole-vector expressions over p, m, v -- *)
    75	adam(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], m: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], v: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], g: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], t: ZZ32, lr: RR64):
    76	    (Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]) = do
    77	    m' = beta1 m + (1 - beta1) g
    78	    v' = beta2 v + (1 - beta2) (g × g)
    79	    p' = p - (lr (m' / (1 - beta1^t))) / (SQRT (v' / (1 - beta2^t)) + epsilon_A)
    80	    (p', m', v')
    81	  end
    82	learningRate(s: ZZ32): RR64 = lr0 (1 - (1.0 s) / nSteps)
    83	
    84	(* --------------------------------------------------- training ----------- *)
    85	run(): () = do
    86	    println "microgpt flat | params " nParams() " | corpus " corpus.size() " x " (blockSize + 1) " | batch 1, 5 steps"
    87	    bsz = 1
    88	    p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] := loadParams(weightsDir, matName, 9, nParams())
    89	    m: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] := zeros(nParams())
    90	    v: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] := zeros(nParams())
    91	    for s <- seq(0#5) do
    92	        t0 = nanoTime()
    93	        (l, g) = step(p, keys(bsz, fn (i: ZZ32): ZZ32 => (s bsz + i) MOD corpus.size()))
    94	        (p, m, v) := adam(p, m, v, g, s + 1, learningRate(s))
    95	        println "step " (s + 1) " loss " l "  (" ((nanoTime() - t0) DIV 1000000) " ms)"
    96	    end
    97	  end
    98	end

     2	   against explorations/apl/reference/hsu-flat/microgpt_concise.dyalog (L6-L30),
     3	   inside apl⦇ … ⦈ over AplMgSyntax + AplMg beside this file, expanding into what
     4	   Run C4 writes by hand (explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss).  The design,
     5	   with the line-by-line table, is DESIGN.md beside this file; the probes that
     6	   settled its two mechanisms are ../probes-4b/PROBES.md.  The array vocabulary
     7	   is FlatArrays2 beside this file (C4's FlatArrays with the sizes in the types
     8	   and the habits of the vocabulary review removed, NOTES-swap.md) and the
     9	   loaders are FlatData2, C4's FlatData over it; every APL
    10	   line expands to C4's own line -- no aplCall, no frame stack, no Any, no
    11	   Object.  Run from explorations/apl/mg: the paths are relative. *)
    12	component MicroGptApl
    13	export MicroGptApl
    14	export Executable
    15	import AplMg.{...}
    16	import AplMgSyntax.{...}
    17	import FlatArrays2.{...}
    18	import FlatData2.{...}
    19	import System.{...}
    20	
    21	(* ------------------------------------------------------------ L6: index
    22	   origin 0 is the base's own; the two hyperparameter lines are host, because a
    23	   top level has no rest for a binding to be the body of.  C4:17-18 verbatim
    24	   but for the APL spellings of the names: a word of two or more uppercase
    25	   letters is a Fortress operator (gaps row 78). *)
    26	(Ne, Blk, Nh, Hd, Vs, Bos) = (16, 16, 4, 4, 27, 26)
    27	(Eps, Lr0, B1, B2, Epsa, Nsteps) = (10.0^(-5), 0.01, 0.85, 0.99, 10.0^(-8), 1000)
    28	(corpusPath, weightsDir) = ("../reference/dzaima/docs.txt", "../reference/dzaima/w")
    29	
    30	(* ^T on a matrix and on every plane of a rank-3 array, over FlatArrays2's two
    31	   transposes, declared here and not in the vocabulary because an api cannot
    32	   declare a postfix operator (gaps row 133); C4:23-24 verbatim.  The APL text
    33	   reaches the same two functions through the grammar's ⍉ rule, which writes a
    34	   call, because ^T may not follow one (rows 144, 158). *)
    35	opr (m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\])^T[\nat r, nat c\]: Matrix[\RR64,c,r\] = transpose(m)
    36	opr (t: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\])^T[\nat a, nat b, nat c\]: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,c,0,b\] = transpose(t)
    37	
    38	(* ------------------------------------------------------ L7, L8: the four
    39	   vector functions are host, C4:27-34 verbatim -- a dfn body is out of the
    40	   focused subset, and the function IS Fortress.  The causal mask is APL. *)
    41	rmsn(x: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = x / SQRT (Eps + (x DOT x) / |x|)
    42	sm(z: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = do e = exp(z - (BIG MAX z)); e / (SUM e) end
    43	Mk = apl⦇ (-10*10)×~(⍳Blk)∘.≥⍳Blk ⦈
    44	rmsn_b(dy: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], x: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = do
    45	    r = SQRT (Eps + (x DOT x) / |x|); y = x / r
    46	    (dy - y ((y DOT dy) / |y|)) / r
    47	  end
    48	sm_b(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], dy: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = p × (dy - (p DOT dy))
    49	
    50	(* ---------------------------------------------------------- L9, L11: the
    51	   layout table and the view are host, C4:37-45 -- a vector of shape pairs is a
    52	   nested array, which no rung of the ladder has *)
    53	matName(i: ZZ32): String =
    54	    if i = 0 then "wte" elif i = 1 then "wpe" elif i = 2 then "lm_head" elif i = 3 then "attn_wq" elif i = 4 then "attn_wk"
    55	    elif i = 5 then "attn_wv" elif i = 6 then "attn_wo" elif i = 7 then "mlp_fc1" else "mlp_fc2" end
    56	matShape(i: ZZ32): (ZZ32, ZZ32) =
    57	    if (i = 0) OR (i = 2) then (Vs, Ne) elif i = 7 then (4 Ne, Ne) elif i = 8 then (Ne, 4 Ne) else (Ne, Ne) end
    58	matCount(i: ZZ32): ZZ32 = do (r, c) = matShape(i); r c end
    59	matOffset(i: ZZ32): ZZ32 = SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#i] matCount(j)
    60	nParams(): ZZ32 = matOffset(9)
    61	view(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], i: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = do (r, c) = matShape(i); view(p, matOffset(i), r, c) end
    62

    64	   corpus is host, C4:48 -- characters and the system alphabet are outside the
    65	   sub-language.  Its two integer arrays are read AS THEY ARE: keys are ZZ32
    66	   throughout the focused base, so there is no conversion anywhere. *)
    67	corpus: Corpus = loadCorpus(corpusPath, Blk, Bos)
    68	Tokm = corpus.tokm
    69	Len = corpus.len
    70

    72	   The three adapters vw h u are ordinary TYPED local functions, as C4:54-55
    73	   are, because a name in APL text is a call of a typed host function now, not
    74	   a push on a frame stack; a view of the flat vector, rank 4 and its inverse

    76	   not separate two statements when the next line can continue the one above,
    77	   and the program's strand names are exactly the ones that continue a line. *)

    81	    u(t: Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = unheads(t, Nh)

    84	      X←wte[ids;]+wpe[pos;] ⋄ Xp←rmsn⍤1⊢X ⋄ X1←rmsn⍤1⊢Xp ⋄
    85	      Q K Vv←X1∘(+.×⍉)¨wq wk wv ⋄ Qh Kh Vh←h¨Q K Vv ⋄
    86	      A←sm⍤1⊢Mk+⍤2⊢(Qh+.×⍤2⊢⍉⍤2⊢Kh)÷Hd*0.5 ⋄ Hc←u A+.×⍤2⊢Vh ⋄
    87	      X2←Xp+Hc+.×⍉wo ⋄ X3←rmsn⍤1⊢X2 ⋄ M0←X3+.×⍉f1 ⋄ Mr←0⌈M0 ⋄ X4←X2+Mr+.×⍉f2 ⋄
    88	      Pr←sm⍤1⊢X4+.×⍉lm ⋄ loss←-(+/vm×⍟tg⌷⍤0 1⊢Pr)÷nv ⋄
    89	      dL←(vm÷nv)×⍤0 1⊢Pr-tg∘.=⍳Vs ⋄ gLM←(⍉dL)+.×X4 ⋄ dX4←dL+.×lm ⋄
    90	      gF2←(⍉dX4)+.×Mr ⋄ dM0←(dX4+.×f2)×M0>0 ⋄ gF1←(⍉dM0)+.×X3 ⋄ dX3←dM0+.×f1 ⋄
    91	      dX2←dX4+dX3(rmsn_b⍤1)X2 ⋄ gWO←(⍉dX2)+.×Hc ⋄ dH←h dX2+.×wo ⋄
    92	      dVh←(⍉⍤2⊢A)+.×⍤2⊢dH ⋄ dS←(A(sm_b⍤1)dH+.×⍤2⊢⍉⍤2⊢Vh)÷Hd*0.5 ⋄
    93	      dQh←dS+.×⍤2⊢Kh ⋄ dKh←(⍉⍤2⊢dS)+.×⍤2⊢Qh ⋄ dQ dK dV←u¨dQh dKh dVh ⋄
    94	      gWQ gWK gWV←X1∘(+.×⍨⍉)¨dQ dK dV ⋄ dX1←(dQ+.×wq)+(dK+.×wk)+dV+.×wv ⋄
    95	      dXp←dX2+dX1(rmsn_b⍤1)Xp ⋄ dX←dXp(rmsn_b⍤1)X ⋄
    96	      gWTE←(⍉ids∘.=⍳Vs)+.×dX ⋄ gWPE←(⍉pos∘.=⍳Blk)+.×dX ⋄
    97	      gr←⊃,/,¨gWTE gWPE gLM gWQ gWK gWV gWO gF1 gF2 ⋄ loss gr ⦈
    98	  end

   102	   three modified assignments are three bindings and a three-name strand.  The
   103	   step counter stays ZZ32, as C4:79's exponent is. *)
   104	adam(P: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], M: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], V: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], gr: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], t: ZZ32, lr: RR64):
   105	    (Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]) =
   106	    apl⦇ Mn←(B1×M)+(1-B1)×gr ⋄ Vn←(B2×V)+(1-B2)×gr*2 ⋄ Pn←P-lr×(Mn÷1-B1*t)÷Epsa+(Vn÷1-B2*t)*0.5 ⋄ Pn Mn Vn ⦈

   110	   write to an outer name.  The step number is widened once in host code, as

content.content:
- P-154 **A list is ordered only where its element type is totally ordered.** The library's `List` extends its lexicographic order only where its element type extends `StandardTotalOrder` (conditional extension, P-151). Floats and `QQ` are only partially ordered, since NaN, and `QQ`'s 0/0, compare with nothing. So on the compiled checker a list of floats or of `QQ` has no order: no `<`, `CMP` or the other comparisons, though its `=` stays. A pair of floats stays ordered: the curator accepted that mismatch as a cost of the list rule. The tuples' own rule is not decided here. No lexicographic trait over partially ordered elements is added now: the team never wrote one, and the case touches neither the distance to the switch-over nor microGPT. Why: the team's `LexicographicOrder` computes `CMP` on its elements as a total comparison, which only totally ordered elements give (`a874948ac:Library/FortressLibrary.fss:1735-1741`), and the team's `List` extended it at every element type (`a874948ac:Library/List.fsi:67`); conditional extension, a `where` form that the team wrote (P-151), reconciles the two. Row 774: walk's half, since walk still gives every list an order; it waits until walk runs the checker (P-12) or row 364, walk's typing of a generic at its argument's run-time class, is fixed.
- F-229 **`array1` and `array2` give a vector and a matrix only at the eight number types, chosen by a `typecase` over a witness of their result type; at any other element type they give a plain array.** The branches are `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64`; each builds the array at that type and returns it through `cast`, in `additiveIdentity`'s shape. `Array1` and `Array2` are invariant, so a branch matches only its own number type exactly. `Number` and `AnyIntegral` get a plain array, since `Vector[\Number,n\]` is not well-formed under the element bound `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }` of `Vector` and `Matrix` (F-151). The specification's "Array Expressions" makes an array of `Number` elements a vector (row 729, contested). Under walk, a type parameter inferred from a `ZZ32` value is `Int`, the one type that `ZZ32` comprises (row 364), and one inferred from a `ZZ64` or `RR64` value is that value's run-time class. Such a type parameter gets a plain array, where the specification gives a vector (row 721). The witness is of the result type because at `T = Int` a witness of the element type, `() -> Int`, would match the `ZZ32` branch, and the `cast` of the `ZZ32` vector to an array of `Int` would throw `CastError`, as `openRange` does (row 722). Gated under walk by `tests/ArrayFactoryNumberTypes` and `ArrayFactoryAbstractNumber`. The distance stage measures the compiled checker's acceptance; it reports, and does not turn the gate red. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-factories/REPORT.md` sections 1 (the change), 3 and 4 (the ways measured).

BIG SQCUP[\Type\] [t' <- gent.typeExtends] findGenType(t')
    end

(** Returns a supertype of given type object that has a proper test generator,
    other than "constructed" one like `genAnyOf`.

    This routine is required for this kind of generic proprety:
    {{{
        propSomething[\T\](l:List[\T\], x:T): Boolean
    }}}
    If `T` were `Float`, a subtype of `RR64`, then `Arbitrary` factory would
    return `genRR64` which covers all values of `Float`, but `List[\Float\]` is
    not type-compatible to `List[\RR64\]` and we will get the unification error.
    Instead we have to convert every instances of `Float` to `RR64` at the first
    time --- this routine does so. **)
private adaptType(arb:ReflectiveArbitrary, t:Type): Type =
    if gen <- arb.genFromType(false, t) then
        if t2 <- findGenType(typeOf(gen)) then
            t2
        else
            fail("genFromType returned a non-generator " gen)
        end
    else
        t
    end

### (c) The operations answered by each path's run time, under one binding

10. **What it is.** The library keeps each declaration with a bare body that names the compiled path's existing helper: `ilkName` on `stringOps.typeName`, `asString` on `stringOps.defaultAsString`, `SEQV` on `equality.sEquiv`. The compiled path calls the helper, as it does today. Walk's loader holds a table of these names and answers each with walk's own operation, the glue classes of today, which call `FValue.seqv` and `type()`. This is how a JVM treats an intrinsic: the method has a Java body, and the virtual machine runs its own code for it [10].
11. **Measured, prototype C.** Walk's half is eight lines in a copy of `NativeApp.java`: a map of three names and a look-up before the loader reads the string. With the three library bindings naming the helpers, in copies of the two library files, the program of section 2.2 printed what the plain build prints, line for line; a control on the plain build stopped at the copy's binding, 'Native helper com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.equality.sEquiv: no Java type carries the declared type of parameter a.' The compiled half needs no change: the same strings compile and run today (section 1, point 12). No class of `nativeHelpers/` gains a dependency, and every method of `stringOps` and `equality` already maps to Fortress (F-321) [11].
12. **What P-58's form then means.** The library's text keeps P-58's form: each body is exactly `builtinPrimitive("…")` naming a static helper, and the checker checks it against the helper's Java signature (F-298). Walk's half departs: for these names walk's loader runs its own operation and does not load the named helper. The helper is the definition of the operation, and walk's operation must answer as it does. Today they do not (section 2.4), so this option needs the meaning first, with a test on both paths that holds them together [12].
13. **Its limits.** Two implementations stay, one in each run time, as the team built them. The compiled helper alone gives `false` for two equal numbers (section 2.3, point 9), so `equality.sEquiv` must answer the meaning for numbers, tuples and strings before the compiled path reads the one library [13].
14. **Files and lines.** Walk: `interpreter/glue/NativeApp.java:196-205`, a table, and the glue classes `ObjectPrims.java` and `AnyPrim.java`, kept as walk's operations. Compiled: none for the move; `nativeHelpers/equality.java:15-18` for the meaning. Both: the three strings. **Tests**: as for (a), and a walk test that each table name runs walk's operation. **Size**: one rung, and the meaning's rung. **The model**: none of its calls [14].
15. **The mirror form.** The bindings could keep their glue strings, with the compiled path mapping each glue name to its helper. That keeps a glue class's name in the library's text, against P-58's form, so it is weaker than (c) [15].

### (d) The three left on glue until walk runs the checker (P-12)

3:Take (e1) with (c): write `Object`'s `asString` in the library as `self.ilkName`, P-91's rule as text, which leaves two natives and keeps the one library's `Object` clear of row 321's recursion on the compiled path; bind `ilkName` and `SEQV` bare to the compiled path's existing helpers `stringOps.typeName` and `equality.sEquiv`, and let walk's loader answer those two names with walk's own operations, as the specification makes `SEQV` the language's own, as walk and the type group each answer it in their run time, and as Java, Swift and Julia answer identity and a value's type; this move keeps every value of walk, as prototype C showed, changes nothing on the compiled path, which runs those helpers today, and needs no carrier of `Any` at all. It takes two decisions not taken: whether P-58's walk half admits a loader that answers a named helper with its own operation, and, before the compiled path reads the one library, what `SEQV` means, where the review proposes the specification's rule (values of different types never equivalent, floats by their bits, tuples element by element, references by identity), which the Working Draft states, whose first part the type group's family shares, and from which walk's earlier code of 2008 departs, with strings and `ZZ` for the curator, and with `equality.sEquiv` and walk's value classes each brought to that meaning under one test on both paths, six lines of the team's `sequivTest.fss` changing with it. If you can keep your objects when all others
Are losing theirs and blaming it on you;
If you can trust your replicas when others
Fail, and vital data van’shes from view
If you can wait and not time-out while waiting
Or, being queued, not offer-up neglect
And when partitioned, plan for the re-mating,
And set the world to rights on reconnect

If you can dream that systems will be faster
If you can think—and not make thoughts your aim;
If you can meet with triumph and disaster
And live to bring the data back again;
If you can bear to hear the truth you’ve spoken
Twisted by competitors who drool
Or watch the Store you gave your life to: broken!
And patch it up again with Norton Tools

If you can make one heap for all your objects
And risk it on one scan of mark-and-sweep,
And lose, and start again to do the collect
And never to the user even beep;
If you can force your disk and net and CPU
To run for years although they’re obsolete,
And so go on when there is nothing in you
Except the Will which says to them: “Complete!”

If you can talk with crowds of eager clients,
And serve the IBMs with SNA;
If neither power surge nor blackout hurts you;
If all men count on you, and know they may;
If you can fill the unforgiving minute
With sixty million methods called and run
Yours is the Earth and everything that’s in it,
